title: Built a dual-module trend-following EA for gold/BTC aimed at FTMO challenges — formal risk-of-ruin sizing, heavy internal audit process. Looking for holes, not selling anything.
author: Vast_Mushroom_5982
selftext:
**Context.** MT5 EA, targeting FTMO 2-step challenges and funded accounts. I don't have a live funded track record yet — this is a research project I've been hard-auditing for months, and I want outside eyes on the logic before I trust it with real capital. Posting because I'd rather find the flaws here than find them live.

**Architecture**  
Two independent long-only trend modules run on the same account. One trades a daily-bar breakout channel across gold and BTC. The other trades a shorter-timeframe breakout on gold only, gated by a real-yield (US 10y TIPS) filter, so it skips gold breakouts when the macro backdrop is actively hostile. Both use ATR-scaled stops. No averaging down, no martingale, no grid. A giveback ratchet locks in part of an open trade's profit once it's run far enough, without hard-capping the upside.

**Position sizing**  
Not fixed-fractional. Size scales with the account's distance above a floor set above the actual prop-firm breach line — risk shrinks automatically as equity nears the constraint (never fully to zero) and expands as a cushion rebuilds. Loosely inspired by Grossman & Zhou (1993) and Zhou & Shang (2015) on drawdown-constrained portfolio choice, but tested empirically rather than taken on faith. I also tried a variant where the floor trails the equity peak instead of staying fixed — it looked better in a simplified replay, but full-cost testing showed it cut both profit *and* drawdown by \~40%+ with no Sharpe improvement, because a trailing floor shrinks size on unrealized profit inside a still-open position, and a closed-trade-only simulation can't see that. Dropped it. Keeping this in because it's a decent example of a model artifact that would have looked like an improvement if I hadn't gone back to full-friction testing.

**Prop-firm compliance layer**  
Hard daily and max-drawdown flattens set tighter than the actual limits, as a buffer against slippage and gaps. A "target lock" flattens and freezes entries once equity clears the profit target, so the system can't gamble away a pass — audit found (and fixed) a real bug where it could latch permanently *below* the actual target if a weekend gap meant the triggering position eventually realized under the line, because the lock checked equity at trigger time rather than the balance actually evaluated at reset. Fixed, not yet forward-validated. Separately: real prop-firm limits are fixed dollar amounts against initial capital, not a percentage of current equity — most EAs size risk off current equity, which drifts out of sync with the real dollar limit as the account compounds. Built an optional cap for this; implemented but not stress-tested, so it ships off by default.

**Process, to keep myself honest**  
Every parameter change is pre-registered — expected outcome written down before I look at results, specifically to stop myself retrofitting a story afterward. Ideas get a cheap power-screen before a full run, and anything that survives gets adversarial review. Two independent outside AI reviews of the code and results, cross-checked against the actual logs — one got its arithmetic exactly right but most of its qualitative interpretations wrong (e.g., treating several independent yearly restart tests as one compounding equity curve), which was itself a useful lesson in how easy MT5 tester output is to misread. Several proposed additions that looked good in a simplified engine died under full-cost, full-friction testing: pyramiding, a faster/ensemble variant, shorter lookback channels.

**What I won't claim**  
No statistical significance established. Ran a deflated Sharpe ratio check against the number of variants I've implicitly tried, and it doesn't clear a bar I'd call rigorous — so this is "plausible edge, unproven," not "proven edge." All results are in-sample/backtest, on a genuinely small number of trade events (this is low-frequency), which means a disproportionate share of total profit sits in a handful of trades — concentration risk I can't size my way out of. The real-yield gate on the gold module is still an open question: cheap simplified testing prefers it off, full-cost testing with real financing prefers it on. Unresolved. No live funded track record.

**What I'm not posting**  
Exact parameters (channel lengths, ATR multipliers, risk percentages, thresholds), the source, or account-level numbers. Not because Donchian breakout is secret — it isn't, it's Turtle-era public domain — but a parameter set with no forward track record attached is noise, and I don't want this read as something to copy-trade or as a solicitation.

**What I'm actually asking**

* Where would you expect a system like this to fail first — regime shift, under-modeled costs/slippage, confirmation bias in my own review process, something else?
* Anyone run trend systems on real (non-sim) prop-firm accounts — does daily-reset mechanics or actual spread/swap behavior surprise you in ways backtests don't capture?
* Is a deflated-Sharpe bar the right falsification test for a low-frequency breakout system, or is there a better one I should be using before risking capital?

No link, no invite code, nothing for sale. Want the logic stress-tested by people who'll actually try to break it.

comments.author: QuanTradin
comments.body:
the two modules aren't really independent on the days that matter. a daily gold breakout and a shorter timeframe gold breakout tend to fire together, so on a gap down you're carrying both stops on the same metal at once.

I'd run the floor logic off combined open gold risk, and check it against the daily loss limit as well as the max loss line, because the daily one is what usually ends a challenge.
